newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares close higher after credit policy.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares close higher after credit policy.

text.p: Share prices finished higher on Tuesday partly helped by the central bank's new credit policy which set the ground for cuts in lending rates, brokers said.

Markets were preoccupied with ongoing efforts to form a fresh United Front (UF) alliance government under a new leader. Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's UF coalition was defeated last week, and Congress party demanded Deve Gowda's removal as a condition for its support.
Concern over the fate of the widely-acclaimed pro-growth budget of the fallen government, which will be debated in parliament next week, also overshadowed the central bank's looser credit stance.
The benchmark Bombay index ended 57.72 points, or 1.61 percent, higher at 3,647.44.
The National exchange index gained 11.65 points, or 1.16 percent to 1,014.90.
But for lingering political uncertainty and the fate of a pro-business budget the market would have perked up sharply, they said.
"Definitely, we would have seen a more positive response to the credit policy but for the political situation," said Antony Sequeira, managing director at Arcadia Share and Stock Brokers.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) loosened its credit policy for the first half fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) to bring down interest rates and keep economic growth on track while reining in inflation.
It scrapped reserve requirements for banks on inter-bank borrowings and cut deposit rates on short-term deposits to 9.0 percent from 10.0 percent.
State-run Corporation Bank cut its prime lending rate to 14 percent from 14.5 percent following the policy statement, and traders expect more banks to follow suit.

"I think interest rates will come down, because the steps taken in this policy will lead to an increase in the lendable resources of banks," RBI Governor C. Rangarajan told Reuters Television in an interview.
Bank have been allowed to invest five percent of their incremental deposits in shares. Earlier the ceiling included investments in debentures and bonds.
The new policy also allowed banks to give bridge loans to companies against shares as the firms awaited to raise capital through a public issue.
"The policy is very optimistic, favourable to corporate, primary market," said Rajesh Bajaj, a director at Calcutta brokerage Lohia Securities Ltd.
He said the full impact of the policy was offset by the political uncertainty and a spate of holidays.
Major exchanges are closed on Wednesday and Friday for religious festivals. It was also closed on Monday for a national holiday.
